Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

derivations.claim: Each nonzero remainder has degree smaller than its divisor by [F1], so the chain terminates. The Euclidean algorithm preserves the common divisors of $f$ and $f'$, and their gcd is $1$ by the square-free hypothesis; hence the last nonzero member is a nonzero constant. A nonzero polynomial has only finitely many real roots: repeatedly divide by $t-c$ at each distinct root $c$ in $\mathbb R[t]$; each division lowers degree, so there can be no more roots than the original degree.

For each intermediate index $0<j<m$, the division identity is $f_{j-1}=q_jf_j-f_{j+1}$. If $f_j(c)=0$, then $f_{j-1}(c)=-f_{j+1}(c)$. No two consecutive members can vanish at one point: the identity would propagate a common zero to the final nonzero constant. Thus both neighbors are nonzero and have opposite signs at $c$.

A polynomial $h$ with $h(c)\ne0$ keeps its sign in some interval about $c$: division by $t-c$ gives $h(t)=h(c)+(t-c)k(t)$, and the finite polynomial $k$ is bounded on $[c-1,c+1]$ by the sum of the absolute values of its coefficients times the corresponding powers of $|c|+1$. Taking $|t-c|$ small enough makes $|(t-c)k(t)|<|h(c)|$. Therefore, near a zero $c$ of an intermediate $f_j$, its two neighboring members keep their opposite signs; whether $f_j$ is positive, negative, or zero, those three entries contribute exactly one sign change. Intermediate zeros do not change $V$, including at an endpoint where $f_0$ is nonzero.

If $c$ is a root of $f_0=f$, then $f_1(c)=f'(c)\ne0$: otherwise the Euclidean algorithm and [F1] give polynomials $u,v\in K[t]$ with $uf+vf'=1$, and evaluating at $c$ would give $0=1$. Division in $\mathbb R[t]$ gives $f(t)=(t-c)h(t)$ by [F6]. Expanding $h$ in powers of $t-c$, the coefficient of $(t-c)$ in $f$ is $h(c)$; the formal derivative formula [F2] says this coefficient is $f'(c)$. By step 3.1, $h$ keeps the sign of $f'(c)$ near $c$, so $f$ changes sign exactly once there, from the opposite sign to the same sign as $f'(c)$. The first pair $(f_0,f_1)$ therefore loses exactly one sign change as $t$ passes left to right through $c$.

The chain has finitely many roots by step 1.1. Every chain member is a real polynomial and so is continuous by [F4]; if its sign changed between two consecutive zeros, [F5] would give an additional zero. Thus between the finitely many chain-root locations all signs are fixed by [F6]. At every intermediate-member zero the variation is unchanged by step 3.1, and at every root of $f$ it decreases by one by step 4.1. Since $f(a)f(b)\ne0$, neither endpoint is a root of $f$; summing the changes from $a$ to $b$ gives $V(a)-V(b)$ equal to the number of distinct roots of $f$ in $(a,b)$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$

derivations.claim: The Euclidean gcd in [F1] terminates because each nonzero remainder has smaller degree by [F3]. By induction on degree, [F5] and [F3] factor $p$ over the field $\mathbb C$ [F10]: take a root, divide by its linear factor, and repeat on the lower-degree quotient. At a root of multiplicity $m$, write $p(z)=(z-\zeta)^m h(z)$ with $h(\zeta)\ne0$. Differentiation by [F4] gives $p^{(j)}(\zeta)=0$ for $j<m$ and $p^{(m)}(\zeta)=m!h(\zeta)\ne0$. Also $p'$ has multiplicity exactly $m-1$ at $\zeta$, so $p/\gcd(p,p')$ contains that root once. Thus the square-free reduction and finite derivative test in [F1] preserve exactly the distinct roots and return their original multiplicities.

Put $M=\max_{j<n}|a_j/a_n|$ for a degree-$n$ polynomial. If $|z|>1+M$, then $|z|>1$ and $\sum_{j<n}|a_jz^j|\le |a_n|M\sum_{j<n}|z|^j=|a_n|M\frac{|z|^n-1}{|z|-1}<|a_n||z|^n.$ Hence $p(z)\ne0$. The exact comparisons and increasing rational enumeration in [F1] therefore find a strict rational bound; any rectangle whose two half-widths exceed that bound contains every root in its interior.

For nonconstant square-free $q$, each root has finite real and imaginary coordinates, so only finitely many vertical or horizontal offsets pass through a root. Only finitely many horizontal offsets can make $\operatorname{Im}q(t+iy)$ identically zero as a polynomial in $t$: otherwise every coefficient polynomial in $y$ would vanish identically, which would force $\operatorname{Im}q(x+iy)$ to be the zero bivariate polynomial; writing $q$ first on the real axis and then differentiating its coefficient expansion in $y$ shows this is impossible for nonconstant $q$. The vertical case is identical. Each vertex condition $\operatorname{Im}q(\pm X\pm iY)=0$ is the zero set of a nonzero polynomial in $(X,Y)$. A nonzero bivariate polynomial cannot vanish on an open rectangle: fixing one coordinate on an interval makes each coefficient polynomial in the other coordinate vanish on an interval and hence identically. The finitely many forbidden coordinate lines and vertex zero sets thus cannot fill the open rational search region $X,Y>B$. Rational pairs are dense there, so the outer-bound enumeration in [F1] finds an admissible rectangle.

On each edge, simultaneous vanishing of $R$ and $I$ is equivalent to a root of their gcd. The vertex test excludes endpoint roots, so [F2] decides whether such a root lies in the edge interior. At each zero of $I$, boundary-root-freeness implies $R\ne0$; the sign of this exact nonzero algebraic value is decidable by refinement, and the square-free Sturm sequence isolates every zero of $I$. Thus every crossing and its direction in [F1] is finitely and exactly determined.

`REALROOTS` is correct at each subdivision by [F2]: its square-free polynomial first records any roots at $-1$ and $1$, divides out those endpoint linear factors using [F3], and applies Sturm to the residual, whose endpoints are root-free. The selected interior cut is not a root, so the two open children partition the residual roots. The polynomial has finitely many distinct roots by repeated division and degree decrease [F3]. If there are at least two, the minimum separation of its finite root set is positive in the real order [F11]; repeated bisection eventually makes every positive-count interval narrower than both that separation and the requested width. Each level has finitely many intervals, so the recursion terminates and outputs disjoint isolators for all real roots in $(-1,1)$, together with the endpoint roots tested separately.

In a parent rectangle already satisfying the admissibility tests, the same finite-exclusion argument gives an admissible cut pair in the product of the two middle-third intervals. Cut coordinates that pass through roots are finite in number; offsets making an edge imaginary restriction identically zero are finite; vertex-zero conditions along an old side are nonzero univariate polynomials because that side's imaginary restriction is not identically zero; and conditions at a new cut intersection are nonzero bivariate polynomials by the argument in step 1.3. Their finite union has empty interior. The exhaustive dyadic enumeration therefore finds cuts for which all four child boundaries satisfy the exact tests.

Let $\gamma(t)=q(z(t))$ traverse an admissible rectangle counterclockwise. Each edge restriction is polynomial, avoids zero, has nonzero imaginary-part polynomial, and has no endpoint with zero imaginary part. It therefore meets the positive real ray only at the finitely many interior zeros isolated in step 1.4. For $w\notin[0,\infty)$, define $\operatorname{Arg}_+(w)$ as the unique $\theta\in(0,2\pi)$ in its polar representation; existence follows by applying [F8] to $-w$ and adding $\pi$. This branch is continuous: on each open semicircle avoiding the cut, the unit-circle parametrization is one-to-one, and the chord identity $|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_0}|=2|\sin((\theta-\theta_0)/2)|$ shows that nearby circle points have nearby angles. Thus on every subarc between positive-ray intersections, $\operatorname{Arg}_+(\gamma(t))$ is continuous. At an upward crossing its one-sided values approach $2\pi$ and $0$, so adding $2\pi$ to the subsequent branch continues the lift and increases its integer offset by one. A downward crossing decreases the offset by one, and a non-crossing contact leaves it unchanged. The curve is closed and its starting vertex is off the ray, so the lifted argument's total increment divided by $2\pi$ is exactly the signed crossing sum in [F1].

For nonzero real $h$, `REALROOTS` returns all roots in $[-1,1]$ by step 1.5, and [F9] shows that its `SIGNCERT` samples determine the sign on each intervening open gap; the root values themselves are zero and the endpoints are tested separately. Thus the routine accepts exactly when $h\ge0$ on the whole interval. The $h=0$ branch accepts directly.

Step 1.1 factors $q(z)=c\prod_j(z-\zeta_j)$ over its distinct roots. Continuous argument lifts add under multiplication, so the winding increment of $q$ is the sum of the increments of these linear factors. Fix one root $\zeta$ not on the rectangle boundary. Enumerate rational directions $(r,s)$ with $(r,s)\ne(0,0)$ by increasing positive denominator and then numerator pair, and take the first whose line is not parallel to a rectangle side and whose line through $\zeta$ contains no rectangle vertex. Only finitely many directions are forbidden, while rational directions are dense, so this search terminates. Normalize the chosen vector to a unit scalar $u$; its norm is nonzero. Rotating the curve $z-\zeta$ by the constant unit scalar $\overline u$ does not change its total argument increment, and makes the chosen direction the positive real ray. If $\zeta$ is inside the convex rectangle, the ray leaves it exactly once; counterclockwise orientation puts the interior on the left, so this outward crossing is upward and contributes $+1$. If $\zeta$ is outside, the ray either misses the rectangle or enters and exits it, contributing a downward crossing and an upward crossing whose signs cancel. Thus the winding increment of $z-\zeta$ divided by $2\pi$ is $1$ exactly for an interior root and $0$ otherwise. Summing over the distinct roots shows that the signed crossing count of $q$ in step 2.2 is exactly the number of roots inside the rectangle. Since $q$ is square-free, this is the number of distinct roots.

A cut line contains no root by step 2.1, and each parent boundary is root-free by admissibility. The four child interiors therefore partition the parent's roots without omission or duplication; their exact counts are correct by step 3.1. Discarding count-zero children and continuing preserves exactly the roots inside the initial rectangle, which contains all roots by step 1.2.

Each subdivision cut lies strictly inside the corresponding middle third, so each child's side lengths are at most $2/3$ of its parent's. The finite set of distinct roots has a positive minimum pairwise distance when it has at least two elements. After finitely many levels, every rectangle has diameter below that separation and below $2^{-b}$; hence it cannot contain two roots. If there is one root, only the precision condition is needed. The finite four-child tree then terminates. Every retained rectangle contains exactly one root, their open interiors are pairwise disjoint, and step 1.1 supplies the correct multiplicity.

derivations.claim: Since $s^2=1-x^2$, direct multiplication gives $W_R^*=W_R$, $W_R^2=I$, and $\det W_R=-1$. Hence $W_R$ is unitary for every allowed $x$.
We prove the polynomial form by induction on $d$. For $d=0$, $U_\Phi=Z(\phi_0)$, so $P=e^{i\phi_0}$ and $Q=0$ satisfy the degree and parity bounds and $PP^*=1$.

By [F2] and [F4], $\overline{e^{i\phi}}=\cos\phi-i\sin\phi=e^{-i\phi}$; by [F3], $e^{i\phi}e^{-i\phi}=1$. Thus $Z(\phi)^*Z(\phi)=I$ and $\det Z(\phi)=1$. Each factor $W_RZ(\phi)$ is unitary with determinant $-1$, so the $d$ signal factors give $U_\Phi^*U_\Phi=I$ and $\det U_\Phi=(-1)^d$.

Write a $2\times2$ unitary matrix as $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&e\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. The cofactor formula gives $M^{-1}=\epsilon\begin{pmatrix}e&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$; equating this to $M^*$ yields $e=\epsilon\overline a$ and $c=-\epsilon\overline b$. Applying this with $\epsilon=(-1)^d$ shows the displayed lower row is forced by the first row.

Suppose the representation holds at degree $d$. Multiplying on the right by $W_R(x)Z(\phi_{d+1})$ gives $P_{d+1}=e^{i\phi_{d+1}}(xP_d+(1-x^2)Q_d)$ and $Q_{d+1}=e^{-i\phi_{d+1}}(P_d-xQ_d)$. Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$.

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $0\ne f=\sum_i a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **degree** is the largest natural number $n$ for which $a_n\ne0$, and its **leading coefficient** is $a_n$:

$$ \deg f:=\max\{i\in\mathbb N:a_i\ne0\},\qquad \operatorname{lc}(f):=a_{\deg f}. $$

The maximum exists because the nonempty support is finite. The polynomial $f$ is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(f)=1_R$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. Accordingly, every degree statement below explicitly separates the zero polynomial rather than assigning it a formal degree.

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $f\in F[x]$, and let $0\ne g\in F[x]$. There are unique polynomials $q,r\in F[x]$ such that

$$ f=qg+r,\qquad r=0\ \text{or}\ \deg r<\deg g. $$

The statement includes $f=0$ and nonzero constant divisors.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

$f(z)=0$, then $f(\overline z)=0$.

and

If $a+bi\ne0$, then

derivations.claim: If $A=0$, choose $B=C=0$. Otherwise evenness makes $\deg A=2n$ for some $0\le n\le d$. By [F3], [F8], and repeated use of [F4], factor $A$ over $\mathbb C$ into its finite multiset of roots with multiplicity.

The root multiset, with multiplicities, is invariant under $\zeta\mapsto-\zeta$ because substituting $-x$ preserves the order of a zero, and under conjugation because $A$ has real coefficients and [F6] applies. The multiplicity at zero is even because every nonzero coefficient of an even polynomial has even exponent. Every real root $s$ with $0<|s|<1$ has even multiplicity: write $A(x)=(x-s)^m h(x)$ with $h(s)\ne0$. Division by $x-s$ gives $h(x)-h(s)=(x-s)k(x)$ for a polynomial $k$. On a bounded interval around $s$, $k$ is bounded (each of its finitely many monomials is bounded); choosing the interval small enough makes $|h(x)-h(s)|<|h(s)|$, so $h$ has the sign of $h(s)$ there by [F9]. If $m$ were odd, $(x-s)^m h(x)$ would then have opposite signs on the two sides of $s$, contrary to $A\ge0$.

Pair the roots into the following classes, choosing one representative from each symmetric class. A zero root of multiplicity $2r$ contributes $x^r$. A real pair $\pm s$ with $0<s<1$ and multiplicity $m$ at each root contributes $(x^2-s^2)^{m/2}$; this is a polynomial because $m$ is even. A real pair $\pm s$ with $s\ge1$ and multiplicity $m$ contributes $R_s(x)^m$, where $R_s(x)=\sqrt{s^2-1}\,x+i s\sqrt{1-x^2}$ and $R_sR_s^*=s^2-x^2$. A pure-imaginary pair $\pm ib$ with $b>0$ and multiplicity $m$ contributes $I_b(x)^m$, where $I_b(x)=\sqrt{b^2+1}\,x+i b\sqrt{1-x^2}$ and $I_bI_b^*=x^2+b^2$.

A nonreal quadruple $\pm a\pm ib$ with $a,b>0$ and common multiplicity $m$ contributes $Q_{a,b}(x)^m$. Put $u=a^2+b^2$ and $v=2(a^2+1)b^2+(a^2-1)^2+b^4$, and set $c=u+\sqrt v$. Since $\sqrt v\ge|a^2-1|$, the two cases $a^2\le1$ and $a^2\ge1$ give $c\ge1$, so all displayed square roots are real by [F5]. Define $Q_{a,b}(x)=c x^2-u+i\sqrt{c^2-1}\,x\sqrt{1-x^2}$. For $x\in[-1,1]$, its quartic norm is $Q_{a,b}(x)\overline{Q_{a,b}(x)}=|Q_{a,b}(x)|^2\ge0$; because the quartic roots are the nonreal numbers $\pm a\pm ib$, it is strictly positive on the real interval. Direct expansion gives $Q_{a,b}Q_{a,b}^*=x^4+2(b^2-a^2)x^2+(a^2+b^2)^2$, the product of the four linear root factors.

Let $G(x)$ be the product of the nonnegative real factors associated with these root classes: $x^{2r}$ for zero roots, $(x^2-s^2)^m$ for interior real pairs, $(s^2-x^2)^m$ for exterior real pairs, $(x^2+b^2)^m$ for pure-imaginary pairs, and the quartics from step 1.4. Then $A=\kappa G$ for a nonzero real constant $\kappa$, because both sides have the same roots with the same multiplicities and the same degree. Enumerate reduced rationals in $(-1,1)$ by increasing positive denominator and then increasing numerator, and take the first $x_0$ outside the finite root set; this search terminates because a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots by step 1.1. There $A(x_0)>0$ by the nonnegativity hypothesis and $A(x_0)\ne0$, and $G(x_0)>0$ by its displayed factors, so $\kappa=A(x_0)/G(x_0)>0$ by [F9]. Let $K=\sqrt{\kappa}$ by [F5].

Multiply the corresponding root-class factors defined above to form $W(x)=K\prod R(x)$, retaining the interior and zero factors as real factors. Repeated use of $(B+i\sqrt{1-x^2}C)(D+i\sqrt{1-x^2}E)=(BD-(1-x^2)CE)+i\sqrt{1-x^2}(BE+CD)$ shows that $W=B+i\sqrt{1-x^2}C$ for real polynomials $B,C$. Their factor identities give $WW^*=A$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Both $WW^*=B^2+(1-x^2)C^2$ and $A$ are polynomials; their difference vanishes at infinitely many real points, so it is the zero polynomial, since a nonzero polynomial has at most its degree many roots by repeated division by linear factors.

In each root class, the real part and the coefficient of $i\sqrt{1-x^2}$ have opposite parities; a real zero or interior factor has only a real part. The multiplication rule in step 3.1 preserves this parity relation. If $\deg A=2n$, the degrees of the factors give $\deg B\le n$ and $\deg C\le n-1$: every imaginary term contains at least one factor whose imaginary coefficient has degree at least one below that factor's real degree. When $n=d$, the pair has a unique parity profile $b$ determined by its nonzero component: $B$ has parity $b$ if $B\ne0$, and otherwise $C$ has parity $1-b$. If $b\ne d$, then $B$ has degree at most $d-1$, while $C$, whose parity is $d$, has degree at most $d-2$; both terms of $B^2+(1-x^2)C^2$ would then have degree at most $2d-2$, contradicting $\deg A=2d$. Thus $b=d$ and the required parities hold.

If $n<d$, let $b$ be the parity profile from step 4.1. If $b\ne d$, multiply $W$ by $x+i\sqrt{1-x^2}$. Its conjugate product is $x^2+(1-x^2)=1$, and the multiplication rule changes the profile from $b$ to $1-b$. It raises the degrees by at most one, so the new bounds are $\deg B\le n+1\le d$ and $\deg C\le n\le d-1$. If $b=d$, no adjustment is needed. This also covers $B=0$ or $C=0$, since the profile is read from the nonzero component. Thus the resulting $B,C$ meet the required bounds and parities, completing the identity.

$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

For every real $x$, both series
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$$
converge absolutely. Equivalently, both power series have infinite radius of convergence.

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x,\quad \cos(\pi/2-x)=\sin x,\quad \sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\quad \cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x,$$
and the quarter-turn and reflection formulas are
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad \cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad \sin(-x)=-\sin x,\quad \cos(-x)=\cos x.$$
On the common natural domains of the two sides,
$$\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x,\quad \cot(\pi/2-x)=\tan x,\quad \sec(\pi/2-x)=\csc x,\quad \csc(\pi/2-x)=\sec x,$$
and
$$\tan(\pi-x)=-\tan x,\quad \cot(\pi-x)=-\cot x,\quad \sec(\pi-x)=-\sec x,\quad \csc(\pi-x)=\csc x.$$
The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $x\in[-1,1]$, put $s(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ using the nonnegative real square root, and define the Hermitian-reflection signal matrix
$$W_R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&s(x)\\s(x)&-x\end{pmatrix}.$$
For each real $\phi$, define $Z(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi})$. For an integer $d\ge0$ and real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$, the length-$d$ QSP sequence is the ordered matrix product
$$U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j)\bigr),$$
where the product is written left to right in increasing $j$ and matrix multiplication acts right to left. For $d=0$ this is $Z(\phi_0)$. This definition fixes the sign of the off-diagonal signal entry, both endpoint phases, and the product order.

The phases are in matrix order: when the factors are applied as chronological circuit layers, the rightmost factor acts first, in accordance with [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. In the ordered signal basis, if both coordinates are nonzero, applying $Z(\phi)$ multiplies the ratio of the second coordinate to the first by $e^{-2i\phi}$; if either coordinate is zero, that relative phase is undefined, while the displayed matrix action remains defined. This is the relative phase convention fixed by [[def-qc-relative-phase]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of

First compute rational sine and cosine approximations at any rational
$m\in[0,2]$ to absolute error $\epsilon>0$. For each series, retain at least
the terms through index $2$ and use the recurrence of successive terms.
Subsequent absolute-term ratios are at most $1/2$ and decrease: for cosine
they are $m^2/((2k+1)(2k+2))$, and for sine they are
$m^2/((2k+2)(2k+3))$. Twice the first omitted absolute term bounds the tail.
Increment the index until this rational bound is at most $\epsilon$.
The geometric decrease gives $O(1+\log^+(1/\epsilon))$ terms and arithmetic
operations, uniformly in $m$. The returned partial sums $c,s$ therefore satisfy
$|c-\cos m|,|s-\sin m|\le\epsilon$.

The integral formula and $\arctan1=\pi/4$ in [F4] give
$1/2<\pi/4<1$: on the two cells of the partition $0,1/2,1$, the decreasing
integrand has lower sum $\tfrac12(4/5+1/2)=13/20>1/2$ and upper sum
$\tfrac12(1+4/5)=9/10<1$. Thus $2<\pi<4$. First check the coordinates
for exact zero; an axis input takes instruction 2 of the algorithm. Otherwise
set $a=|u|$, $b=|v|$ by exact comparisons and signs, and initialize
$[L,U]=[0,2]$. It contains $\theta$ by [F1] and $\pi/2<2$. While its width
$w=U-L$ exceeds $h/8$, set $m=(L+U)/2$, $\epsilon=w/96$, and compute $c,s$
as in step 1.1. Form the exact algebraic number $q=bc-as$.
If $q>2\epsilon$, replace $L$ by $m$. If $q<-2\epsilon$, replace $U$ by
$m$. Otherwise replace the bracket by
$[L,U]\cap[m-12\epsilon,m+12\epsilon]$.
These are two exact comparisons against rational buffers; equality belongs
to the third branch. No comparison with an exact transcendental value is made.

Let $D=b\cos m-a\sin m=\sin(\theta-m)$ by [F3]. Since
$a,b\in[0,1]$, $|D-q|\le(a+b)\epsilon\le2\epsilon$. Also
$|\theta-m|\le2$ because $\theta,m\in[0,2]$. By [F2], the sign of $D$
is the sign of $\theta-m$, and $|\theta-m|\le3|D|$.
Thus either definite comparison in step 1.2 retains $\theta$ and halves the
bracket. In the third branch, $|D|\le4\epsilon$ implies
$|\theta-m|\le12\epsilon$, so the intersection also retains $\theta$ and
has width at most $24\epsilon=w/4$. It is nonempty. Every iteration contracts
by at least a factor $1/2$, independently of how close the unknown phase is
to a midpoint.

The loop terminates in $O(1+\log(1/h))$ iterations, returning rational
$L,U$ containing $\theta$ with $U-L\le h/8$. Its comparison count is linear
in the number of iterations. In an iteration with width $w>h/8$, step 1.1
needs $O(1+\log(1/h))$ rational operations. The total is therefore
$O((1+\log(1/h))^2)$. The exact algebraic numbers compared are only rational
linear combinations of the fixed coordinates $a,b$. No algebraic-coordinate
approximation, root isolation, normalized-vector division, or sensitivity
bound occurs in these instructions.

Obtain a rational enclosure $I_\pi$ for $\pi$ of width at most $h/8$ by
Machin's identity $\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$. For completeness,
put $\alpha=\arctan(1/5)$, $\beta=\arctan(1/239)$. The integral in [F4]
gives $0<\beta<\alpha<1/5$, so
$0<4\alpha-\beta<4/5<1<\pi/2$ by step 1.2. Sine/cosine addition and their quotient give
$\tan(2\alpha)=5/12$, $\tan(4\alpha)=120/119$, and
$\tan(4\alpha-\beta)=(120\cdot239-119)/(119\cdot239+120)=1$.
Injectivity of the principal tangent gives $4\alpha-\beta=\pi/4$.
For each arctangent, consecutive alternating partial sums enclose its value,
and their separation is at most $5^{-(2N+1)}$ after the first $N$ terms.
Choose $N$ by incrementing until $20\cdot5^{-(2N+1)}\le h/8$ and take the
outward linear combination of the two enclosures. This uses
$O(1+\log(1/h))$ rational operations. All displayed denominators are positive;
all angles in these tangent identities are in its nonsingular principal range.

On an axis, the explicit OP0 branches build $J$ as follows: if $v=0,u>0$,
use $[0,0]$; if $v=0,u<0$, use $I_\pi$; if $u=0,v>0$, use $I_\pi/2$;
if $u=0,v<0$, use $-I_\pi/2$. The zero vector is excluded by the unit promise
(the general atan2 procedure returns INVALID there). No angular bisection is
needed on an axis. Otherwise use the exact signs of $u,v$ to build a rational
interval $J$ for a phase $\phi$ of $u+iv$: if $u>0,v>0$ use $[L,U]$; if $u<0,v>0$ use
$I_\pi-[L,U]$; if $u<0,v<0$ use $-I_\pi+[L,U]$; if $u\ge0,v<0$ use
$-[L,U]$. Reflection, quarter-turn and parity identities give
$u+iv=e^{i\phi}$, and $\operatorname{width}(J)\le h/4$.
Let $t_0$ be its rational midpoint. Choose the least nonnegative integer $k$
with $2^{-k}\le h/16$ by repeated halving, and round $t_0$ to a multiple of
$2^{-k}$, obtaining $t$ with $|t-t_0|\le h/16$. Thus
$|t-\phi|\le3h/16\le3/16$. The exponential series and [F5] imply
$|e^{it}-e^{i\phi}|\le\sum_{n\ge1}|t-\phi|^n/n!
\le |t-\phi|/(1-|t-\phi|)\le3h/13<h$.
The phase lies in a fixed bounded interval, so this dyadic $t$ has
$O(1+\log(1/h))$ bits. The constructed interval $J$ and rounding bound are
the certificate.

Put $z=e^{it}-ω$. By [F5] and [F6], $Z(t)-Z(φ)$ has diagonal entries
$z,\overline z$. On a vector with orthonormal coordinates $x_0,x_1$,
its squared output norm is $|z|^2(|x_0|^2+|x_1|^2)$. Thus every unit vector
has output norm $|z|$, and the operator norm is exactly $|z|<h$. Together
with the operation counts and termination above, this proves all claims.

For every $x\in[-1,1]$ and phase list $\Phi$ of length $d+1$, $U_\Phi(x)$ is unitary with determinant $(-1)^d$. There are polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix},$$
where $P=0$ or $\deg P\le d$ with parity $d$, $Q=0$ or $\deg Q\le d-1$ with parity $d-1$, and $PP^*+(1-x^2)QQ^*=1$ as a formal polynomial identity.

Put $s=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $W_R=\begin{pmatrix}x&s\\s&-x\end{pmatrix}$, $W_S=\begin{pmatrix}x&is\\is&x\end{pmatrix}$, and $C=Z(\pi/4)$. Then
$$CW_RC=iW_S^\dagger,\qquad W_S^\dagger=Z(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2).$$
For $d\ge1$, define $U_S(\Psi)=Z(\psi_0)\prod_{j=1}^d(W_SZ(\psi_j))$. If $\Psi$ is the SU(2)-convention phase list with $\psi_0=\phi_0+\pi/4$, $\psi_j=\phi_j-\pi/2$ for $1\le j<d$, and $\psi_d=\phi_d-3\pi/4$, then
$$U_R(\Phi)=i^dU_S(\Psi).$$
The affine phase-list map is invertible. The scalar $i^d$ is part of the identity: in a control-first block $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ it acts on the active control branch and cannot be discarded as a global phase.

Every $z\ne0$ has a unique representation $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $r=|z|>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]].
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

Let $F$ be a field, let $f\in F[x]$, and let $0\ne g\in F[x]$. There are unique polynomials $q,r\in F[x]$ such that

$$ f=qg+r,\qquad r=0\ \text{or}\ \deg r<\deg g. $$

The statement includes $f=0$ and nonzero constant divisors.

Let $x\in[-1,1]$, put $s(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ using the nonnegative real square root, and define the Hermitian-reflection signal matrix
$$W_R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&s(x)\\s(x)&-x\end{pmatrix}.$$
For each real $\phi$, define $Z(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi})$. For an integer $d\ge0$ and real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$, the length-$d$ QSP sequence is the ordered matrix product
$$U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j)\bigr),$$
where the product is written left to right in increasing $j$ and matrix multiplication acts right to left. For $d=0$ this is $Z(\phi_0)$. This definition fixes the sign of the off-diagonal signal entry, both endpoint phases, and the product order.

derivations.claim: If the pair comes from a phase list, [[lem-qa-23-phase-sequence-unitarity]] gives exactly the stated matrix form, degree/parity bounds, and polynomial identity for the sequence defined in [F8]. This proves the forward implication.

Let $d=0$ and suppose the pair is admissible. Then $Q=0$ and $P$ is constant with $|P|=1$. Set $\phi_0=\operatorname{Arg}(P)$ from the unique principal polar representation [F4]; [F5] gives $P=e^{i\phi_0}$. By [F8], $U_\Phi=Z(\phi_0)=\operatorname{diag}(P,P^*)$, the required matrix.

Let $d=1$. Parity gives $P=ax$ and $Q=b$ for constants $a,b\in\mathbb C$. Evaluating the identity at $x=0$ and $x=1$ gives $|b|=|a|=1$. Set $\alpha=\operatorname{Arg}(a)$ and $\beta=\operatorname{Arg}(b)$ by [F4], so [F5] gives $a=e^{i\alpha}$ and $b=e^{i\beta}$; then set $\phi_0=(\alpha+\beta)/2$, $\phi_1=(\alpha-\beta)/2$. By the order in [F8], direct multiplication of $Z(\phi_0)W_R(x)Z(\phi_1)$ gives entries $ax$, $s(x)b$, $s(x)\overline b$, and $-x\overline a$, exactly the four entries in the Statement for $d=1$.

Now let $d\ge2$ and assume the converse has been constructed at every smaller nominal degree. Put $P_S=i^{-d}P$ and $Q_S=i^{-(d+1)}Q$. Multiplication by unit complex scalars preserves the bounds, parities and coefficient-conjugate identity in [F1]. The corresponding source-convention matrix is $M_S(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P_S(x)&i s(x)Q_S(x)\\i s(x)Q_S^*(x)&P_S^*(x)\end{pmatrix}.$ For real $x$, its diagonal entries in $M_S^*M_S$ are $|P_S|^2+s^2|Q_S|^2=1$, and its off-diagonal entries cancel as $-i sP_S^*Q_S+i sQ_SP_S^*=0$ and its conjugate. Also $W_S^*W_S=I$ and $\det W_S=1$ by direct multiplication using $x^2+s^2=1$, while every $Z(\psi)$ is unitary with determinant $1$ by [[lem-qa-23-phase-sequence-unitarity]]. Thus the peel multiplies by unitary matrices.

If $P_S$ is constant, then the identity at $x=1$ gives $|P_S|=1$. For every $x\in(-1,1)$ it then gives $(1-x^2)|Q_S(x)|^2=0$, hence $Q_S(x)=0$ throughout that interval. If $Q_S$ were nonzero of degree $m$, choose $m+1$ distinct points in $(-1,1)$; repeated division by their linear factors using [F7] would force a divisor of degree $m+1$ of $Q_S$, contradicting [F6]. Thus $Q_S=0$. The parity of the nonzero constant $P_S$ forces $d$ even. Set $\psi_0=\operatorname{Arg}(P_S)$ by [F4], so [F5] gives $P_S=e^{i\psi_0}$. Direct multiplication using $x^2+s^2=1$ gives $W_SZ(\pi/2)W_S=Z(\pi/2)$ and therefore $W_SZ(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2)=I$. This identity is the length-two phase product $Z(0)W_SZ(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2)$. Insert it on the left of the current sequence; the adjacent $Z(-\pi/2)$ and initial $Z(\psi_0)$ combine to $Z(\psi_0-\pi/2)$ by [F3], so the result is again a standard phase list and has two additional signal factors. Repeating this $d/2$ times pads the constant sequence to nominal degree $d$.

Otherwise let $\ell=\deg P_S\ge1$, with leading coefficients $p_\ell$ for $P_S$ and $q_m$ for $Q_S$. The identity forces $Q_S\ne0$ and $m=\ell-1$: if $m\ge\ell$, the highest term of $-(x^2)Q_SQ_S^*$ has degree $2m+2>2\ell$ and cannot cancel; if $m<\ell-1$, the degree-$2\ell$ term $|p_\ell|^2x^{2\ell}$ cannot cancel. At degree $2\ell$, the coefficients therefore satisfy $|p_\ell|^2-|q_{\ell-1}|^2=0$. Thus $r:=p_\ell/q_{\ell-1}$ has modulus one. Set $\psi_d=\operatorname{Arg}(r)/2$ using [F4]; then [F5] gives $e^{2i\psi_d}=r$.

Multiply $M_S$ on the right by $Z(-\psi_d)W_S^*$, where $W_S=\begin{pmatrix}x&is\\is&x\end{pmatrix}$. The result has the same form with $P'=e^{-i\psi_d}xP_S+e^{i\psi_d}(1-x^2)Q_S,\qquad Q'=e^{i\psi_d}xQ_S-e^{-i\psi_d}P_S.$ The possible degree-$(\ell+1)$ coefficient of $P'$ and degree-$\ell$ coefficient of $Q'$ both equal zero by $e^{2i\psi_d}=p_\ell/q_{\ell-1}$. Their parities then give $\deg P'\le\ell-1$ and $\deg Q'\le\ell-2$, the bounds for nominal degree $d-1$. The right multiplier and $M_S$ are unitary with determinant $1$, so their product $N=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ is also unitary with determinant $1$. The cofactor formula gives $N^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}D&-B\\-C&A\end{pmatrix}$, whereas unitarity gives $N^{-1}=N^*=\begin{pmatrix}A^*&C^*\\B^*&D^*\end{pmatrix}$. Equating entries yields $D=A^*$ and $C=-B^*$. Since $A=P'$ and $B=i sQ'$, this is the required lower row $[i s Q'^*,P'^*]$. If $a=e^{-i\psi_d}$, then $P'=axP_S+\overline a(1-x^2)Q_S$ and $Q'=\overline a xQ_S-aP_S$; expanding their coefficient-conjugate products cancels the two mixed terms and leaves $P'P'^*+(1-x^2)Q'Q'^*=(x^2+1-x^2)\bigl(P_SP_S^*+(1-x^2)Q_SQ_S^*\bigr)=1.$ So $(P',Q')$ is admissible at nominal degree $d-1$.

The pair in step 2.1 is admissible at nominal degree $d-1$, so the induction hypothesis supplies its finite phase list. Since $M'=M_SZ(-\psi_d)W_S^*$, reversing the multiplication gives $M_S=M'W_SZ(\psi_d)$; append $\psi_d$ to that list. Equivalently, repeated application strictly lowers the nominal degree and reaches one of the explicit $d=0$ or $d=1$ bases. This constructs a finite source-convention phase list.

For $d\ge2$, apply the inverse affine phase map in [F3] to obtain a reflection phase list $\Phi$. Since $U_R(\Phi)=i^dU_S(\Psi)$, its upper-left entry is $i^dP_S=P$, its upper-right entry is $i^{d+1}sQ_S=sQ$, and its lower entries are $(-1)^{d+1}sQ^*$ and $(-1)^dP^*$. Thus it is the required reflection sequence and the converse follows. Together with the forward implication and both base cases this proves the equivalence for all $d\ge0$.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $A\in\mathbb R[x]$ be even, of degree at most $2d$, and nonnegative on $[-1,1]$. Then there are $B,C\in\mathbb R[x]$ such that
$$A(x)=B(x)^2+(1-x^2)C(x)^2,$$
where $\deg B\le d$, $\deg C\le d-1$, $B$ has parity $d$, and $C$ has parity $d-1$. The zero polynomial is both even and odd and satisfies every degree bound.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

derivations.claim: Put $R=1-p^2$. Since $p(-x)=(-1)^dp(x)$, $p^2$ and hence $R$ are even. Its degree is at most $2d$, and the interval bound on $p$ gives $R(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$.
Apply [F1] to obtain real polynomials $B,C$ with $R=B^2+(1-x^2)C^2$, degree bounds $d,d-1$, and parities $d,d-1$.

Define $P=p+iB$ and $Q=C$. By [F3], $P^*=p-iB$ and $Q^*=C$, so $PP^*=p^2+B^2$ and $QQ^*=C^2$. Their sum in the admissibility identity is therefore $p^2+B^2+(1-x^2)C^2=p^2+R=1$. The degree bounds and parities of $p,B,C$ also give the required bounds and parities of $P,Q$; hence the pair is admissible by [F2].
For real $x$, the real part of $P(x)=p(x)+iB(x)$ is exactly $p(x)$. Thus the uniform error is zero and is at most every $\delta>0$.

OP1's source SU(2) completion packages an $i$ in its off-diagonal coefficient; this item keeps $Q=C$ for the reflection signal. Step 6 forms the corresponding source-normalized pair, and step 7 maps the complete phase list back using [[lem-qa-23-hermitian-signal-convention-conversion]], including its scalar $i^d$. Never use one convention's off-diagonal formula with the other's phases.

6. **Peel phases.** Form $P_S=i^{-d}P$ and $Q_S=i^{-(d+1)}Q$, and initialize an empty peel list. For nominal degree $n=d,d-1,\ldots$, if $P_S$ is constant, verify $Q_S=0$ and $|P_S|=1$, verify that $n$ is even, and store the base phase scalar $P_S$. Initialize the residual source phase-scalar list with $[P_S]$. To pad to degree $n$, prepend $n/2$ length-two identity blocks $W_SZ(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2)=I$; represent each block by phase scalars $(1,i,-i)$ and merge adjacent phase scalars by multiplication in matrix order. An odd constant case returns CERTIFICATE_ERROR. Otherwise let $\ell=\deg P_S$, read leading coefficients $a_\ell,b_{\ell-1}$, verify $b_{\ell-1}\ne0$ and $|a_\ell|=|b_{\ell-1}|$, and put $r=a_\ell/b_{\ell-1}=x+iy$. In efficient-numerical mode choose $\omega_n=i$ when $x=-1$; otherwise construct the positive tower root $s=\sqrt{(1+x)/2}$ with known upper bound $1$ and set $\omega_n=s+i y/(2s)$. It has unit modulus and square $r$ by [[lem-qa-23-qsp-completion-peel-arithmetic-cost]]. In the other modes call `ROOTS(z^2-r,1)` and choose its first lexicographic descriptor. Either square-root choice makes the exact leading-term cancellation valid. Set $e^{i\psi_n}=\omega_n$, append $\omega_n$ to the peel list with index $n$, and update:

   $$P_S\leftarrow e^{-i\psi_n}xP_S+e^{i\psi_n}(1-x^2)Q_S,\qquad Q_S\leftarrow e^{i\psi_n}xQ_S-e^{-i\psi_n}P_S,$$

   using the old right-hand sides simultaneously. Verify the coefficient identity after each peel. The cancelled leading terms lower the nominal degree by one. Return CERTIFICATE_ERROR if any exact check fails. The loop terminates after at most $d$ peels.

7. **Convert and approximate phases.** Append the reverse of the indexed peel list to the residual base phase-scalar list to obtain the source phase scalars $\zeta_0,\ldots,\zeta_d$ in matrix order. If $d=0$, take the sole reflection phase scalar to be $\omega_0=\zeta_0$. If $d\ge1$, convert them to reflection phase scalars by the inverse map in [[lem-qa-23-hermitian-signal-convention-conversion]]: set $\omega_0=e^{-i\pi/4}\zeta_0$, set $\omega_j=i\zeta_j$ for $1\le j<d$, and set $\omega_d=e^{3i\pi/4}\zeta_d$. These are exact algebraic multiplications by eighth roots of unity and require no transcendental angle extraction; retain the exact scalar $i^d$ in controlled use. For each $\omega_j$, call [[alg-qa-23-certified-phase-approximation]] with tolerance $\delta_0/(16(d+1))$; return its rational angle and distance certificate. If a finite-basis phase compiler is separately supplied, pass it those angles and require a unitary output with further operator error at most $\delta_0/(16(d+1))$ for each phase; return IMPLEMENTATION_ERROR if it cannot supply that bound. Without such a compiler, output the exact algebraic phase scalars and continuous-rotation list with finite-basis compilation marked not applicable.

**Output and failure branches.** On `SUCCESS`, return $\Phi$, the exact $B,C$ identity certificate, every leading-coefficient/root certificate, the numerical phase certificates, and the actual arithmetic, query, gate, precision and output-cost ledger. `INVALID` means the input promise failed. `CERTIFICATE_ERROR` means an exact generated or supplied identity check failed. `IMPLEMENTATION_ERROR` means the optional finite-basis compiler could not certify its allocated per-phase error. In efficient-numerical mode, without a supplied complement or optional compiler, the full construction and its continuous-rotation phase certificates require $\operatorname{poly}(d,1+\log_+(1/\delta))$ operations in the declared exact-algebraic arithmetic model, by [[thm-qa-23-qsp-synthesis-correctness]]. Complete modes assert finite termination rather than that uniform bound; supplied-certificate reading and optional compiler work remain separately charged. No bare existence choice, free root oracle, free phase gate implementation, or finite Turing complexity claim is made.

The coefficient model is the exact algebraic model: coefficients and algebraic roots are represented by defining polynomials and rational isolators, with exact addition, multiplication, inversion of nonzero values, conjugation, equality, order, and real-sign decisions. Every such operation is charged as one exact algebraic operation. The algorithm makes no bit-complexity claim. A root descriptor consists of its defining square-free polynomial, an isolating rectangle containing exactly that root, and its multiplicity; exact algebraic operations refine these descriptors when needed.

`ROOTS(p,b)` takes a nonzero $p(z)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jz^j\in\mathbb C[z]$ with rational or exact-algebraic coefficients and an integer $b\ge1$. The zero polynomial returns `INVALID`; a nonzero constant returns the empty root list.

1. Compute $g=\gcd(p,p')$ by monic Euclidean remainders and set $q=p/g$. The polynomial $q$ has each distinct root of $p$ exactly once.

2. If $n>0$, put $M=\max_{j<n}|a_j/a_n|$ and enumerate rational $B>1+M$ until the strict inequality is certified. Search rational $X,Y>B$ in increasing dyadic denominator and then lexicographic numerator order until the open rectangle $(-X,X)+i(-Y,Y)$ has no root on its boundary, each vertex value of $q$ has nonzero imaginary part, and the restriction of $\operatorname{Im}q$ to each directed edge is not the zero polynomial. The strict Cauchy bound puts every root inside every such rectangle.

3. To count a rectangle, first certify that its boundary is root-free: on each directed edge restrict $q$ to $F(t)=R(t)+iI(t)$, $0\le t\le1$, and use the exact polynomial gcd and Sturm count to decide whether $R$ and $I$ have a common zero there. Require also that every vertex has nonzero imaginary value and that no edge restriction $I$ is identically zero. If any condition fails for a proposed subdivision, enumerate rational vertical and horizontal cuts in the middle third of the corresponding side ranges, by increasing dyadic denominator and then lexicographic numerator, and use the first pair for which all four child rectangles satisfy these conditions.

4. On each directed edge of an admissible rectangle, isolate every distinct zero of $I$ in $(0,1)$ using the square-free Sturm sequence of $I$. There are no endpoint zeros because the vertices have nonzero imaginary value. At each isolated zero, the boundary-root certificate gives $R\ne0$; exact sign refinement decides whether $R>0$ or $R<0$. For $R>0$, add $+1$ if $I$ changes from negative to positive, add $-1$ if it changes from positive to negative, and add $0$ if it does not change sign. For $R<0$, add $0$. The sum over the four counterclockwise edges is the rectangle's distinct-root count.

5. Discard rectangles with count zero. If the count is one and $w_x^2+w_y^2\le2^{-2b}$, where $w_x,w_y$ are its rational side lengths, retain its open interior. Otherwise subdivide by Step 3 and recount the four children. The open interiors are pairwise disjoint and their root-free boundaries ensure no root is omitted or duplicated.

6. For each retained rectangle, find its original multiplicity as the least $m\ge1$ for which $q$ and $p^{(m)}$ have no common root in that rectangle. Test common-root membership by a gcd followed by the same certified rectangle count. This finite derivative test ends by $m=n$, since $p^{(n)}$ is a nonzero constant.

The same carrier supplies `REALROOTS(h)`, used for exact interval-sign checks. For a real nonzero polynomial $h\in K[x]$ with exact real-algebraic coefficients, replace it by its square-free part. Test and record roots at $-1$ and $1$ directly, and divide out each corresponding linear factor once when present; the residual square-free polynomial has root-free endpoints. Isolate its roots in $(-1,1)$ as follows: start with that open interval, use the Sturm variation drop to count roots, discard count-zero intervals, retain count-one intervals once their rational width is at most the requested threshold, and otherwise bisect at the first rational in the middle third that is not a root. Every interval endpoint is kept root-free. A zero polynomial is handled separately by the caller.

`SIGNCERT(h)` decides whether $h\ge0$ throughout $[-1,1]$. If $h=0$, accept. Otherwise check $h(-1),h(1)\ge0$, call `REALROOTS(h)`, and choose one rational sample in each open gap between consecutive root isolators and the endpoints (or $0$ if there are no roots). Accept exactly when every sample value is nonnegative. Exact algebraic comparisons determine all branches. `SIGNCERT` and `REALROOTS` use the same exact operation model and have no hidden numerical zero test.

This is a finite exact-algebraic procedure, not a polynomial-time bit algorithm. The root-separation, boundary-search, sign-certificate, Sturm, and winding-count proofs are supplied by [[thm-qa-23-polynomial-root-isolation-correctness]]. No arithmetic operation count implies a bit bound.

For every nonzero rational or exact-algebraic complex polynomial $p$ and integer $b\ge1$, under the exact algebraic operation model declared in [[alg-qa-23-polynomial-root-isolation]], the algorithm terminates and returns pairwise-disjoint open rational rectangles of Euclidean diameter at most $2^{-b}$, each containing exactly one distinct root and together containing every root. Each rectangle carries the algebraic root descriptor and the original multiplicity. The supplied `REALROOTS` and `SIGNCERT` routines also terminate and return the stated exact real-root and interval-sign certificates. No bit-complexity bound is asserted.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. The sequence defining $f'$ has finite support because the coefficient sequence of $f$ does ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). This is an algebraic operation and does not use a limit.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be
**interior to $A$** ([[def-local-extremum]],
[[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]]). Suppose $f$ has a local extremum at $c$
([[def-local-extremum]]) and is differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]).
Then

$$f'(c) \;=\; 0 .$$

The symbol $f'(c)$ is meaningful under these hypotheses because an interior
point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$, which is proved in
[[def-local-extremum]].

**Interiority is a hypothesis and not a convenience.** At a point of $A$ that is
not interior, the argument below cannot place points of $A$ on both sides of
$c$, and the conclusion genuinely fails: the companion page exhibits a function
on $[0,1]$ attaining both its greatest and its least value at points where the
derivative is $1$.

**No converse is asserted.** A vanishing derivative does not produce an
extremum. The witness is the cubic of
[[fs-vanishing-derivative-forbids-strict-increase]], which has $f'(0) = 0$ and
neither a local maximum nor a local minimum at $0$; that failure is recorded in
the remarks of that item, not as an item of its own.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ have degree at most $d$, parity $d\bmod2$, and $|p(x)|\le1$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Then there is a QSP-admissible pair $P,Q$ of degree bound $d$ such that $\operatorname{Re}P(x)=p(x)$ on $[-1,1]$. In fact, the completion is exact, so for every $\delta>0$ it also satisfies $|\operatorname{Re}P(x)-p(x)|\le\delta$.

For every integer $d\ge0$, a pair $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ is QSP-admissible of degree bound $d$ if and only if there is a real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix}\quad (x\in[-1,1]).$$
The converse is constructive: a leading-coefficient phase peel reduces the degree at each nonconstant stage. The polynomial identity, determinant signs, product order, and phase convention are exactly those in [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]] and [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]].

Given exact algebraic reals $u,v$ with $u^2+v^2=1$ and rational $\eta>0$, let
$h=\min(\eta,1)$. In a model charging one operation for each ideal exact algebraic
field operation and order/equality comparison, the procedure [[alg-qa-23-certified-phase-approximation]] returns a certified
rational angle $t$ with $|e^{it}-(u+iv)|<h$. It requires
$O((1+\log(1/h))^2)$ rational arithmetic operations and
$O(1+\log(1/h))$ exact algebraic operations/comparisons. It does not refine an
algebraic isolator. The rational output has $O(1+\log(1/h))$ bits after a final
dyadic rounding. This is not a claim about algebraic operation implementation,
intermediate rational bit lengths, or Turing time. If $ω=e^{iφ}$, then
$\|Z(t)-Z(φ)\|_{\rm op}=|e^{it}-ω|<h$.

Fix $x\in[-1,1]$ and a length-$d$ sequence from [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]]. Suppose the $j$th implemented phase is a unitary $\widetilde Z_j$ with $\|\widetilde Z_j-Z(\phi_j)\|_{\rm op}\le\zeta_j$, for $0\le j\le d$. With exact signal calls, the implemented product obeys
$$\|\widetilde U_\Phi(x)-U_\Phi(x)\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_{j=0}^d\zeta_j.$$
If the $k$th implemented signal call is also a unitary $\widetilde W_k$ with $\|\widetilde W_k-W_R(x)\|_{\rm op}\le\eta_k$, for $1\le k\le d$, then the right-hand side is $\sum_{j=0}^d\zeta_j+\sum_{k=1}^d\eta_k$. These norm errors do not supply controlled or inverse access; their availability and charge remain part of the declared access model.

Let $x\in[-1,1]$, put $s(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ using the nonnegative real square root, and define the Hermitian-reflection signal matrix
$$W_R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&s(x)\\s(x)&-x\end{pmatrix}.$$
For each real $\phi$, define $Z(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi})$. For an integer $d\ge0$ and real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$, the length-$d$ QSP sequence is the ordered matrix product
$$U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j)\bigr),$$
where the product is written left to right in increasing $j$ and matrix multiplication acts right to left. For $d=0$ this is $Z(\phi_0)$. This definition fixes the sign of the off-diagonal signal entry, both endpoint phases, and the product order.

The phases are in matrix order: when the factors are applied as chronological circuit layers, the rightmost factor acts first, in accordance with [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. In the ordered signal basis, if both coordinates are nonzero, applying $Z(\phi)$ multiplies the ratio of the second coordinate to the first by $e^{-2i\phi}$; if either coordinate is zero, that relative phase is undefined, while the displayed matrix action remains defined. This is the relative phase convention fixed by [[def-qc-relative-phase]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$.

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. In particular, the
one-dimensional zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an ordered subfield with charged ideal exact field operations, equality tests and order tests. Given $p\in K[x]$ of degree at most $d$, whether $|p(x)|\le1$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ can be decided in $O((d+1)^4)$ such operations, without root isolation or coefficient-height assumptions. This is an arithmetic-count claim; implementation bit costs and input encoding/access remain separate.

Let $P$ be a nonzero real rational polynomial of degree $n$. Let $H\ge1$ bound the binary lengths of its integer coefficients after clearing denominators and removing content. The efficient alternate `GRID-ROOTS(P,b)` terminates and has the same root/multiplicity correctness as ROOTS. It uses $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ exact rational arithmetic and comparison operations. No cost for a rational operation is silently identified with its bit cost.

For bounded real $p$ of degree at most $d$ and parity $d\bmod 2$, put $\tau=\min(\delta,8)$ and $\log_+(x)=\max(0,\log x)$. `ROUND-QSP(p,d,δ)` uses $\operatorname{poly}(d,\log_+(1/\delta))$ exact coefficient comparisons and rational arithmetic, and returns a parity-preserving dyadic $h$ with $\|h-p\|_\infty\le5\tau/64<\tau/8$, $\|h\|_\infty\le1-3\tau/64$, and an integer multiple of $1-h^2$ with degree at most $2d$ and coefficient height $O(d\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\delta)+1)$. Consequently its root isolators to $b$ bits cost $\operatorname{poly}(d,\log_+(1/\delta),b)$ arithmetic operations independently of the original coefficient heights in this declared coefficient-access model.

This does not assert polynomial arithmetic complexity for refining the resulting algebraic QSP phases, nor bit complexity for the Euclidean-remainder implementation, nor efficient reading of an arbitrarily long input encoding.

Let $h\in\mathbb Q[x]$ be parity-compatible, of degree at most $d$, with $|h|<1$ on $[-1,1]$. Let $H$ bound the binary lengths of every coefficient numerator and denominator of $R=1-h^2$. Suppose its complete exact root list, multiplicities and fixed-precision rational isolating rectangles are supplied. In a model charging ideal exact algebraic field/order/equality operations and permitting finite extension tower/DAG descriptors, root-class completion and QSP phase peeling use $\operatorname{poly}(d,H)$ operations and polynomially many descriptor nodes and written index bits. Positive roots use counted bisection with known rational upper bounds. Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. The sequence defining $f'$ has finite support because the coefficient sequence of $f$ does ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). This is an algebraic operation and does not use a limit.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.
