e j}(1+|x_k|)\le2^d$; the absolute denominator is $(2/d)^d j!(d-j)!\ge(2/d)^d$. Therefore each coefficient of $L_j$ has absolute value at most $d^d$, and, since $|p(x_j)|\le1$, every coefficient of $p$ has absolute value at most $A=(d+1)d^d$. This interpolation identity follows because subtracting the interpolant leaves a polynomial of degree at most $d$ with $d+1$ distinct zeros. For $d=0$ use $A=1$. Hence $\log_2(\max(2,A))=O(d\log(d+1)+1)$, independently of any encoding of the original coefficients.

Let $\tau=\min(\delta,8)$ and $t=2^{-L}$. The least-$L$ rule gives $t\le\tau/[64(d+1)]$ and, unless $L=0$, $t>\tau/[128(d+1)]$. Since $0<\tau\le8$, the shrink factor $1-\tau/16$ lies in $[1/2,1)$. Bisection on $[-A-1,A+1]$ locates each coefficient of $(1-\tau/16)p$ to a mesh cell using $O(\log(A+1)+L)$ exact comparisons and rational operations; exact comparison at a mesh midpoint resolves a tie without a limit test. Rounding error per coefficient is at most $t/2\le\tau/[64(d+1)]$, so $\|h-(1-\tau/16)p\|_\infty\le\tau/64$. Thus $\|h-p\|_\infty\le5\tau/64<\tau/8$ and $\|h\|_\infty\le1-3\tau/64$. Parity is preserved because forbidden coefficients remain exactly zero. The integers $2^L h_j$ have length $O(L+\log(A+1))$, and the convolution coefficients of $2^{2L}(1-h^2)$ have length $O(L+\log(A+1)+\log(d+1))$. Minimality of $L$ gives $L=O(\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\tau)+1)$, proving the claimed height and rounding cost, also when $\delta\ge1$. Zero leading rounded coefficients only lower the actual degree.

We give explicit coarse separation estimates sufficient for counting subdivisions. For a primitive integer polynomial $U$ of degree $m$ and coefficient magnitude at most $2^J$, every root has $|z|\le C=1+2^J$ by the Cauchy argument: outside that radius the leading monomial strictly dominates the geometric sum of the others. Every primitive integer divisor $V$ of $U$ has leading coefficient dividing that of $U$ and all its roots among those of $U$. Its coefficients, by expanding its linear factors, thus have magnitude at most $2^J2^m\max(1,C)^m$. The assertion that primitive integer divisors may be used here follows from Gauss's lemma: products of primitive polynomials are primitive, since reduction modulo any prime gives a product of two nonzero polynomials over a field; clearing denominators of a rational factorization and comparing contents then gives the integral factorization. Consequently the primitive square-free part, and every gcd with another integer polynomial, has coefficient height $O(m(J+1))$. This is an output coefficient-growth bound; it does not bound the internal Euclidean fractions.

Let $V(z)=az^r+\sum_{j<r}v_jz^j$ be the primitive square-free integer part of $U$, of degree $r\ge2$. Define $W(t)=a^{r-1}V(t/a)$. Its leading coefficient is one, and its $j$-th coefficient for $j<r$ is $v_ja^{r-1-j}$, an integer. Its distinct roots are $\beta_i=a\zeta_i$, with $|\beta_i|\le|a|C$. By [F4], $\operatorname{Disc}(W)$ is a nonzero integer and $|\operatorname{Disc}(W)|=\prod_{i<j}|\beta_i-\beta_j|^2\ge1$. If $\Delta_\beta$ is the least separation of its roots, all other pairwise distances are at most $2|a|C$, so $1\le\Delta_\beta^2(2|a|C)^{r(r-1)-2}$. Therefore the separation of the roots of $V$ obeys $\Delta_\zeta=\Delta_\beta/|a|\ge|a|^{-1}(2|a|C)^{-(r(r-1)-2)/2}$. Step 2.1 bounds $\log_2|a|$ by $O(m(J+1))$ and $\log_2 C$ by $O(J+1)$, so $\log_2(1/\Delta_\zeta)=O(m^3(J+1))$. Constants and degree-one polynomials need no separation estimate. This argument uses only the two actual local discriminant suppliers in [F4], with no resultant multiplicativity premise.

Put $q$ equal to the square-free part of $P$ and $F(x,y)=\operatorname{Im}q(x+iy)$. This is a nonzero real bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $n$: if $\operatorname{Im}q$ vanished everywhere, its $x$ derivative and its $y$ derivative would force $q^{\prime}=0$ by the coefficient expansion, contrary to nonconstancy. A nonzero bivariate polynomial of total degree $\le n$ vanishes at at most $nN$ points of a product of two $N$-point sets. Indeed, if its leading nonzero coefficient as a polynomial in $y$ has $x$-degree $s$, at most $s$ $x$-values annihilate that coefficient; at every remaining $x$ there are at most $n-s$ $y$-zeros, giving at most $sN+(N-s)(n-s)\le nN$. Each fixed old edge restriction of $F$ is nonzero by admissibility, so it has at most $n$ forbidden new vertex coordinates. There are at most $n$ root real coordinates and $n$ root imaginary coordinates, and at most $n$ coordinates making $F$ vanish identically along a vertical or horizontal line: such a coordinate must annihilate any chosen nonzero coefficient polynomial. The new center-vertex condition excludes at most $nN$ pairs. Old-edge vertex, root-line, and identically-zero-edge restrictions together exclude fewer than $20(n+1)N$ pairs. The analogous four outer-corner polynomials $F(\pm X,\pm Y)$ are nonzero and obey the same bound. Therefore $N=100(n+1)$ gives an admissible pair both outside and inside, so `INTERNAL_ERROR` is unreachable. At most $N^2$ candidate pairs are tested at each node. A univariate nonzero polynomial similarly excludes at most $n$ candidates, proving the one-dimensional bounded search.

Every child side length lies between one third and two thirds of its parent side length. The initial side lengths have logarithm $O(H+1)$, by the original Cauchy bound. By step 2.2, after $D=\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ levels every rectangle has diameter less than both $2^{-b}$ and the least distinct-root separation, and hence has count at most one. At every level at most $n$ positive-count rectangles exist, because their disjoint interiors each contain a root by [F2]. Each is replaced by at most four children, so there are $O(n(D+1))$ tested tree nodes, not $4^D$. A side at level $k$ has length at least its initial length times $3^{-k}$. The least dyadic denominator containing $N+1$ middle-third points therefore has exponent $O(H+k+\log(n+1))$; all coordinates have numerator and denominator length $T=O(H+D+\log(n+1))$. Even if the interval already contains many integers, only its first $N$ grid points are tested. This last restriction is essential: unrestricted lexicographic enumeration of all pairs in a very wide interval has no polynomial bound merely from a finite forbidden-coordinate count.

Integer parts and grid generation are charged operations rather than free primitives. For a rational operand of numerator/denominator length at most $S$, find its bounding signed powers of two by doubling, then find its floor by binary search through the bounded integer interval, using $O(S+1)$ rational comparisons and additions; compare exactly with the resulting integer to obtain the ceiling and strict open-interval endpoints. Before denominator clearing, normalize the input $P$ by its nonzero leading coefficient in $O(n+1)$ rational field operations. If $U$ is its primitive integer representative with height $H$, each resulting monic coefficient ratio is $U_j/U_n$, whose reduced numerator and denominator lengths are $O(H)$, independently of an arbitrarily large common rational scalar in the original $P$. The product of these at most $n+1$ denominators has length $O((n+1)H)$; using that product as common denominator gives integer coefficients of length $O((n+1)H)$. Their content is found by integer Euclidean gcds. Each division quotient is obtained by the bounded binary search just described, with polynomial-length integer operands. Integer remainders decrease in magnitude; after at most two nonterminal divisions the larger nonzero operand has at least halved (if the first remainder exceeds half the previous divisor, the next is smaller than its complement). Thus the number of divisions per gcd is linear in the initial operand length. Content removal and denominator clearing therefore cost $\operatorname{poly}(n,H)$ rational arithmetic and comparisons. The resulting primitive integer representative has height at most $H$ and is the input used in steps 2.1–3.2. In particular the outer $B$ is obtained in $\operatorname{poly}(H)$ operations from the original coefficient ratios. To generate a grid, begin with denominator one and double it, recomputing the strict lower/upper admissible integer numerators by this binary search, until their difference gives at least $N+1$ points. Step 3.2 bounds the number of doublings by $O(H+D+\log(n+1))$; every rational tested has polynomial numerator/denominator height in $n,H,b$, because it is a parent coordinate or width times such a dyadic denominator. Each integer-part search therefore costs $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ operations. Writing the first $N$ consecutive grid numerators costs $O(N)$ further additions. This bound also applies to any one-dimensional bounded grid once its coordinate-height and denominator-doubling bounds are established. The least $L$ in rounding is likewise found by sequential denominator doubling and exact comparison with $\tau/[64(d+1)]$, with $O(\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\tau)+1)$ iterations; mesh-cell integer selection is the bounded binary search already charged in step 1.2. No floor, ceiling, or denominator selection is treated as unit-cost.

Each rational edge substitution $z=u+vt$ into $q$ has degree at most $n$. Clearing the rational denominators after binomial expansion gives real and imaginary integer polynomials with coefficient height $J_{\mathrm{edge}}=\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$: each term uses at most $n$ coordinate factors of length $T$ and one $q$ coefficient of height $O(n(H+1))$, and there are at most $n+1$ terms per coefficient. This also applies to all proposed edges, since they use the same bounded-coordinate grids. Products of two such edge polynomials have polynomial degree and height. Their primitive square-free parts and gcds have polynomial output height by step 2.1, and their distinct roots have separation $2^{-\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)}$ by step 2.2. The same facts apply to the gcds used for multiplicity tests, since the $m$-th derivative has coefficient height $O(H+n\log(n+1))$ and its gcd is a divisor of $q$.

Polynomial division of degree-at-most-$n$ rational polynomials takes $O(n^2)$ field operations, and Euclidean and negative-remainder chains have at most $n$ nonzero stages. A Sturm evaluation at rational endpoints thus takes $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ field operations and comparisons, regardless of the rational operand sizes. Square-free reduction and every boundary gcd test have the same polynomial arithmetic bound. Isolate each edge's $I$-roots on $[0,1]$ with the bounded one-dimensional search, first handling endpoint factors. The separation estimate for the square-free product $RI$ proves that $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$ levels suffice to separate distinct $I$-roots and distinguish each $I$-root from all noncommon $R$-roots. A root $\alpha$ of $I$ on the edge is not a root of $R$ by the certified boundary test. Refinement therefore eventually puts $\alpha$ in an interval containing no $R$-root; [F3] certifies this last fact by zero $R$-root count, and a rational sample gives the nonzero sign of $R$ there. The sign change of $I$ is its two endpoint signs. At every level at most $n$ positive $I$-root intervals are retained (at most $2n$ when isolating the product). For a depth-$K$ interval in $[0,1]$, its length is at least $3^{-K}$ and its endpoints have dyadic height $O(K+\log(n+1))$; the grid denominator therefore requires $O(K+\log(n+1))$ doublings. The grid integer parts, ceilings, and written candidate coordinates are consequently charged by step 3.3 within the same polynomial operation bound. Endpoint handling, bounded-grid cuts, all root counts, and all refinements therefore take $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$ rational arithmetic operations. A nonzero constant $I$ has no crossings; an identically zero $I$ was already excluded by the grid.

Combining $O(n(D+1))$ nodes, $N^2$ candidates per node, polynomial edge costs from step 4.2, and at most $n$ derivative/gcd multiplicity tests per retained root proves $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ rational arithmetic cost. All accepted boundaries satisfy exactly the conditions in [F2], so its winding, partition, and multiplicity arguments prove correctness unchanged. Substituting $n\le2d$ and $H=O(d\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\delta)+1)$ from step 1.2 gives the claimed rounded-input root cost. The proof counts field operations; it never bounds Euclidean intermediate operand lengths or the precision required by later algebraic phase calculations, so it makes none of those additional assertions.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $A\in\mathbb R[x]$ be even, of degree at most $2d$, and nonnegative on $[-1,1]$. Then there are $B,C\in\mathbb R[x]$ such that
$$A(x)=B(x)^2+(1-x^2)C(x)^2,$$
where $\deg B\le d$, $\deg C\le d-1$, $B$ has parity $d$, and $C$ has parity $d-1$. The zero polynomial is both even and odd and satisfies every degree bound.

For every integer $d\ge0$, a pair $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ is QSP-admissible of degree bound $d$ if and only if there is a real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix}\quad (x\in[-1,1]).$$
The converse is constructive: a leading-coefficient phase peel reduces the degree at each nonconstant stage. The polynomial identity, determinant signs, product order, and phase convention are exactly those in [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]] and [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]].

Put $s=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $W_R=\begin{pmatrix}x&s\\s&-x\end{pmatrix}$, $W_S=\begin{pmatrix}x&is\\is&x\end{pmatrix}$, and $C=Z(\pi/4)$. Then
$$CW_RC=iW_S^\dagger,\qquad W_S^\dagger=Z(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2).$$
For $d\ge1$, define $U_S(\Psi)=Z(\psi_0)\prod_{j=1}^d(W_SZ(\psi_j))$. If $\Psi$ is the SU(2)-convention phase list with $\psi_0=\phi_0+\pi/4$, $\psi_j=\phi_j-\pi/2$ for $1\le j<d$, and $\psi_d=\phi_d-3\pi/4$, then
$$U_R(\Phi)=i^dU_S(\Psi).$$
The affine phase-list map is invertible. The scalar $i^d$ is part of the identity: in a control-first block $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ it acts on the active control branch and cannot be discarded as a global phase.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: For an exact algebraic $r=x+iy$ with $x^2+y^2=1$, select one square root by:
If $x=-1$, return $\omega=i$ (then necessarily $y=0$). Otherwise put $s=\sqrt{(1+x)/2}>0$, $t=y/(2s)$, and return $\omega=s+it$.

Here $-1<x\le1$, so the positive square root exists, is nonzero, and has
the root-selection description $S^2-(1+x)/2=0$, $0<S<2$ over the existing
real algebraic field. Its two roots are distinguished immediately by sign.
One has $t^2=(1-x)/2$ because $y^2=(1-x)(1+x)$, whence
$s^2+t^2=1$, $s^2-t^2=x$, and $2st=y$. Therefore
$|\omega|=1$ and $\omega^2=r$. The $x=1,y=0$ case returns $1$.
No small-denominator numerical approximation is performed; the division is
exact. There is no conditioning assumption.

This replaces a generic call ROOTS($z^2-r$,1) by a constant number of field
operations and exact comparisons and the explicit quadratic-root descriptor
routine below. It may choose the other square root from the existing
lexicographic-rectangle rule. Either root gives the leading-term cancellation
and an exact factorization: subsequent phases change coherently with that
choice. The efficient-numerical branch explicitly selects this formula, while the complete modes retain their lexicographic choice.

Given an existing exact real algebraic value $A\ge0$ and a known rational
$U\ge\max(1,\sqrt A)$, compare $A$ with zero. If equal, return rational zero.
Otherwise initialize $[l,r]=[0,U]$. While $r-l>1/2$, put $m=(l+r)/2$ and
compare $A$ with $m^2$ exactly. Equality returns the rational value $m$.
If $A<m^2$, put $r=m$; if $A>m^2$, put $l=m$. After the loop, return the
tower descriptor consisting of $T^2-A$ over the existing field and the rational
isolating interval $[l,r]$, specifying its unique nonnegative root.

For $A>0$, the roots are $\pm\sqrt A$, distinct, and only the positive root
belongs to $[0,U]$. The square function is strictly increasing on this
nonnegative interval, so each branch preserves $\sqrt A\in[l,r]$ and excludes
the negative root. Every iteration halves the width and uses $O(1)$ rational
or exact field operations and one exact comparison. Hence the routine uses
$O(1+\log U)$ operations/comparisons and writes a degree-two defining equation
plus its rational isolator. A root at the original right endpoint is permitted
in the closed isolator; the root is still unique. If open endpoints are required,
start with $[0,2U]$; this adds at most one iteration and makes the positive root
interior unless a midpoint equality has already returned it rationally.

For the half-angle radicand $A=(1+x)/2$, one has $0<A\le1$ after the $x=-1$
branch, so $U=1$ is known without search. One bisection suffices for a closed
width-$1/2$ isolator; at most two suffice with the open-endpoint initialization.
This is an actual counted descriptor-construction loop, not a free ROOTS call
or a radical oracle. Subsequent field operations and order/equality queries on
these tower values remain the explicit charged primitives of the declared exact algebraic comparison/field model. These are ideal exact equality/order resources charged per use; their implementation is not supplied by the descriptor loop.

In a model requiring conversion at every step to a rational defining polynomial
and a rational isolator, the quadratic relation has an algebraic coefficient.
Converting it to a rational defining polynomial requires elimination, and
converting all subsequent values into that representation can be expensive.
The descriptor routine does not bound that conversion cost. A tower of $d$
quadratic extensions may have degree $2^d$, even though its construction writes
only $d$ degree-two tower equations and rational isolators.

Suppose the rational completion polynomial $R$ has nonzero coefficient
numerators and denominators of absolute value at most $2^H$. A rational Cauchy
bound $B\ge1$ can be chosen with $B\le2^{2H+2}$, because the leading
coefficient ratio is at most $2^{2H}$. Every classified root coordinate
$s,a,b$ then has absolute value at most $B$. The real exterior and imaginary
radicands are bounded by $B^2$ and $B^2+1\le2B^2$, so $U=2B$ works.
For a quadruple put $D=2(a^2+1)b^2+(a^2-1)^2+b^4$. Then $D\le4B^4+4B^2+1\le9B^4$, so $U=3B^2$ works for $\sqrt D$.
The resulting $c=a^2+b^2+\sqrt D$ is at most $5B^2$, so $U=5B^2$ works
for $\sqrt{c^2-1}$ once its required nonnegativity is established by the
complement supplier. All these descriptor-construction loops therefore use
$O(1+H)$ operations/comparisons per radical. They do not require roots to be
well separated, and they do not approximate the input algebraic coordinates.

Write $N(B,C)=B^2+(1-x^2)C^2$. Expanding the pair multiplication rule gives $N((B,C)(D,E))=N(B,C)N(D,E)$. The factors $(x,0)$, $(x^2-s^2,0)$, $(\sqrt{s^2-1}x,s)$ and $(\sqrt{b^2+1}x,b)$ have norms respectively $x^2$, $(x^2-s^2)^2$, $s^2-x^2$ and $x^2+b^2$. For a quadruple put $A=a^2+b^2$. The radicand in step 3.1 satisfies $D=(A-1)^2+4b^2$, so $b>0$ gives $c=A+\sqrt D>1$. Also $c^2-2Ac-1=-2(a^2-b^2)$. Consequently the pair $(cx^2-A,\sqrt{c^2-1}x)$ has norm $x^4-2(a^2-b^2)x^2+A^2$, the monic polynomial with roots $\pm a\pm ib$. These identities verify the radicands and the norm factors directly. There is also no uncontrolled reciprocal scale hidden in the final $K$.
The squared norms of the unscaled elementary factors are, respectively,
$x^2$, $(x^2-s^2)^2$, $s^2-x^2$, $x^2+b^2$, and the monic degree-four
root polynomial for a quadruple. For the quadruple, the $x^4$ coefficient is
$c^2-(c^2-1)=1$. Thus the product norm $G$ has leading coefficient $+1$ or
$-1$. If $R$ is nonconstant, its leading coefficient is minus the square of
the leading coefficient of the rounded target, and $\kappa>0$ implies
$\kappa=|\operatorname{lc}(R)|$. Hence $\kappa\le2^H$, and one can compute the rational upper bound $U=1+|\operatorname{lc}(R)|\le2^{H+1}$ to construct $K=\sqrt\kappa$; alternatively use the absolute
value of the target leading coefficient directly. If $R$ is a nonzero
constant, $0<R\le1$ and $U=1$ suffices. The unit-norm parity correction
does not alter $G$ or this bound. These estimates count only the quadratic
descriptors after the exact root list has already been obtained; they supply
no bound for generating that root list.

At a nonconstant peel, comparison of the highest coefficients in $PP^*+(1-x^2)QQ^*=1$ forces $\deg Q=\ell-1$ and $|a_\ell|^2=|b_{\ell-1}|^2$, so $b_{\ell-1}\ne0$ and $r=a_\ell/b_{\ell-1}$ is unit. For either unit square root $\omega^2=r$, the leading terms in $P'$ and $Q'$ below are $\overline\omega a_\ell-\omega b_{\ell-1}=0$ and $\omega b_{\ell-1}-\overline\omega a_\ell=0$; parity lowers the resulting degree bounds by one. Direct expansion preserves the admissibility norm identity. The selected root therefore implements the same exact cancellation used for [F2]. Computing it,
selecting the unit root above with its counted tower descriptor, and conjugating
the root are $O(1)$ charged operations/comparisons. The simultaneous coefficient-array
updates $P'=\overline\omega\,xP+\omega(1-x^2)Q$, $Q'=\omega xQ-\overline\omega P$ take $O(n+1)$ field operations at nominal degree $n$. Degree/parity scans
take $O(n+1)$ exact comparisons; there are at most $d$ peels. Thus the peel
itself takes $O((d+1)^2)$ field operations/comparisons, including the $O(d)$
quadratic-root descriptor constructions. If every full polynomial coefficient identity is recomputed
naively after every peel, budget $O((d+1)^3)$ field operations instead;
this remains polynomial. Padding and multiplication by the fixed eighth roots
of unity use $O(d+1)$ additional operations and at most one fixed $\sqrt2$
descriptor construction with $U=2$. The base constant is already a unit algebraic scalar and needs
no Arg oracle.

There are at most $2d$ roots counting multiplicity and therefore $O(d+1)$ elementary complement factors and quadratic descriptors. Schoolbook polynomial-array pair multiplication and final coefficient-identity checks use $O((d+1)^3)$ field operations in total; root classification and symmetry checks use $O((d+1)^2)$ exact comparisons. Each descriptor writes a degree-two equation whose coefficients reference existing nodes, and an isolator of $O(H+1)$ rational bits from its known bounded endpoint. Every field operation writes one referenced node rather than expanding prior expressions. Thus all certificate equations and operation lists have polynomially many nodes, indices and bits in $d,H$; the supplied root descriptors are referenced. These are arithmetic/descriptor costs, and make no claim about implementing the ideal equality/order tests or field operations.
